blocks.text: 1. Vocabulary

blocks.alt: All possible tokens form the vocabulary as a fixed list

blocks.text: Subword Tokenization's own closing recap, already covered in Subword Tokenization, pointed forward here. Vocabulary, exploring how that fixed set of tokens is actually chosen and sized, closes the loop on how tokenization actually gets built.
It is genuinely the concrete, finished list every tokenizer actually draws its tokens from, the exact structure explored in full throughout this topic.

3. From Tokens To A Fixed List

This connects back to Byte Pair Encoding and WordPiece merges, both already covered in Subword Tokenization. Those genuinely merge operations eventually stop, leaving behind one fixed, finished list of tokens.
That genuinely finished list is exactly what gets called the model's own vocabulary, the genuinely concrete output of the whole tokenizer training process explored throughout the rest of this topic.
4. Vocabulary Size Choice

blocks.alt: A small vocabulary is compared against a large vocabulary

blocks.text: This connects back to the vocabulary size tradeoff, already covered generally in Subword Tokenization. Genuinely real vocabularies typically range from tens of thousands to over one hundred thousand tokens.
This genuinely exact number is a deliberate design choice made before training even begins, a genuinely important decision explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 5. Special Tokens

blocks.alt: PAD, UNK, and EOS are example special tokens

blocks.text: This connects back to the vocabulary size choice, already covered in this topic. A genuinely small number of special tokens get reserved for structural roles rather than actual words.
These genuinely mark things like sequence start, sequence end, padding, and unknown tokens, a genuinely small but essential slice of the vocabulary explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 6. Out Of Vocabulary Handling

blocks.alt: An unknown token is mapped to UNK or broken into subwords

blocks.text: This connects back to special tokens, already covered in this topic. Even with subword tokenization, already covered generally in Subword Tokenization, something genuinely rare can still fall outside the vocabulary.
A genuinely reserved unknown token, already covered as a special token, genuinely handles that remaining edge case, a genuinely final safety net explored throughout the rest of this topic.
7. Vocabulary And The Model's Output Layer

blocks.alt: Vocabulary size determines the output layer size

blocks.text: This connects back to the finished list of tokens, already covered in this topic. The model's own final output layer genuinely has exactly one output slot per vocabulary token.

Vocabulary size genuinely directly determines the size of that final output layer, already covered as the probability distribution in Sampling, a genuinely direct, concrete consequence explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 8. Cross Lingual Vocabularies

blocks.alt: Language A and language B can share one vocabulary

blocks.text: This connects back to vocabulary size, already covered in this topic. A genuinely multilingual model's own vocabulary must genuinely cover subword pieces across many different languages at once.
This genuinely tends to push real vocabularies toward the genuinely larger end of that typical range, a genuinely practical consequence of supporting more than one single language.
9. Recognizing Why Vocabulary Size Is Genuinely A Real Design Decision

blocks.alt: Choosing a vocabulary size means balancing coverage and cost

blocks.text: This connects back to a genuinely larger output layer costing more compute, already covered in this topic. Smaller vocabularies, already covered in this topic, directly reduce exactly that output layer cost.

This connects back to fewer tokens per word improving efficiency, already covered generally in Subword Tokenization. Larger vocabularies, already covered, remain genuinely preferable when shorter sequences matter more.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates building a small vocabulary with special tokens, already covered in this topic, and handling an out-of-vocabulary case.

code.content:
# already covered as special tokens in this topic
special_tokens = ["<pad>", "<bos>", "<eos>", "<unk>"]

# already covered as the finished list of tokens in this topic
word_tokens = ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "mat"]

vocabulary = {token: idx for idx, token in enumerate(special_tokens + word_tokens)}
print(f"Vocabulary (already covered in this topic): {vocabulary}")
print(f"Vocabulary size (already covered as the vocabulary size choice in this topic): {len(vocabulary)}")

def encode(word, vocabulary):
    # already covered as out of vocabulary handling in this topic
    return vocabulary.get(word, vocabulary["<unk>"])

sentence = ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "rug"]  # "rug" is genuinely not in the vocabulary
encoded = [encode(w, vocabulary) for w in sentence]

print(f"\nSentence (already covered in this topic): {sentence}")
print(f"Encoded (already covered in this topic): {encoded}")
print(f"\nNote: 'rug' genuinely mapped to the <unk> token ID {vocabulary['<unk>']}, already covered as out of vocabulary handling")

blocks.content: Running this example shows an unseen word correctly falling back to the reserved unknown token ID, exactly the out-of-vocabulary handling already covered in this topic, while every other word maps to its own fixed ID.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Vocabulary is the concrete, finished list of tokens a tokenizer actually draws its tokens from.
Merge operations from Byte Pair Encoding or WordPiece eventually stop, leaving this fixed list behind.
Real vocabularies typically range from tens of thousands to over one hundred thousand tokens.
A small number of special tokens mark sequence start, sequence end, padding, and unknown words.
A reserved unknown token handles rare cases that still fall outside the vocabulary.
Vocabulary size directly determines the size of the model's own final output layer.
Multilingual models tend to need larger vocabularies to cover subword pieces across many languages.
Smaller vocabularies reduce output layer cost; larger vocabularies shorten sequences per word.
